DISABILITY ACCOMMODATION AND THE INTERACTIVE PROCESS AT THE HIRING STAGE (GOV. CODE §§ 12940(M), (N), 12926; GREEN V. STATE OF CALIFORNIA; GELFO V. LOCKHEED MARTIN; SCOTCH V. ART INSTITUTE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about disability accommodation at the hiring stage: the employer duties that the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) states in terms of an "applicant" as well as an "employee," the statutory definitions that frame those duties, and the decisions that describe how the duties work and who must prove what. It draws on Government Code section 12940, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), (e)(2), (m) and (n), and on the definitions in Government Code section 12926, subdivisions (f), (p) and (u); on the California Supreme Court's decision in Green v. State of California (2007) 42 Cal.4th 254, which holds that a FEHA disability-discrimination plaintiff bears the burden of proving he or she is a qualified individual able to perform the essential duties of the position sought or held with or without reasonable accommodation; on Gelfo v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 34, a rescinded-job-offer case holding that the duties to accommodate and to engage in the interactive process run to an applicant whom the employer regards as disabled; and on Scotch v. Art Institute of California-Orange County, Inc. (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 986, which describes what the interactive process is, how it is triggered, and what an individual must identify to recover for a failure to engage in it. Where a specific employer and applicant are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. The sheet reports what the statutes and the decisions say. It does not address whether any particular job function is essential, whether any particular accommodation is reasonable or would produce undue hardship, or whether any particular hiring decision was lawful, and it does not restate the separate rules — covered in other information sheets in this corpus — that govern pre-offer medical examinations and inquiries, post-offer examinations, physical agility testing, or religious accommodation.

THE ACCOMMODATION DUTY IS WRITTEN TO COVER APPLICANTS AS WELL AS EMPLOYEES (GOV. CODE § 12940(M))
FEHA states the reasonable-accommodation duty as an unlawful employment practice, and it states it in terms that name applicants. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (m)(1) makes it unlawful "[f]or an employer or other entity covered by this part to fail to make reasonable accommodation for the known physical or mental disability of an applicant or employee." The same paragraph states the outer limit of the duty: "Nothing in this subdivision or in paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) shall be construed to require an accommodation that is demonstrated by the employer or other covered entity to produce undue hardship, as defined in subdivision (u) of Section 12926, to its operation." Paragraph (2) of the same subdivision makes it a separate unlawful practice for a covered employer, in addition to the protections of subdivision (h), to "retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting accommodation under this subdivision, regardless of whether the request was granted." The word the statute uses is "known": the duty attaches to a "known physical or mental disability." A related provision addresses how an accommodation request can arise before an offer is made. Subdivision (e)(1) generally forbids an employer or employment agency to require a medical or psychological examination of an applicant or to inquire whether an applicant has a disability, but subdivision (e)(2) provides that, notwithstanding that prohibition, "an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant's request for reasonable accommodation."

THE INTERACTIVE PROCESS IS A SEPARATE STATUTORY DUTY, AND IT TOO NAMES APPLICANTS (GOV. CODE § 12940(N))
Government Code section 12940, subdivision (n) makes it an unlawful employment practice "[f]or an employer or other entity covered by this part to fail to engage in a timely, good faith, interactive process with the employee or applicant to determine effective reasonable accommodations, if any, in response to a request for reasonable accommodation by an employee or applicant with a known physical or mental disability or known medical condition." Two features of that text are on its face. The process is owed to "the employee or applicant," and it is triggered "in response to a request for reasonable accommodation." The Court of Appeal has described the resulting duty as independent of the duty to accommodate: in Gelfo v. Lockheed Martin Corp., discussing subdivision (n), the court stated that "[t]he statute provides an independent basis for liability," while also observing that "an employer's duty to accommodate is inextricably linked to its obligation to engage in a timely, good faith discussion with an applicant or employee whom it knows" is disabled and who has requested an accommodation, to determine the extent of the individual's limitations before the individual may be deemed unable to work. Scotch v. Art Institute of California-Orange County, Inc. described the process itself, quoting an earlier decision: "The ‘interactive process’ required by the FEHA is an informal process with the employee or the employee’s representative, to attempt to identify a reasonable accommodation that will enable the employee to perform the job effectively." The same passage adds that "Ritualized discussions are not necessarily required."

WHAT "ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS" MEANS, INCLUDING FOR A POSITION THE APPLICANT ONLY DESIRES (GOV. CODE § 12926(F))
Because the accommodation duty and the statutory exceptions both turn on the "essential duties" or "essential functions" of the position, FEHA defines the term. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (f) provides: "‘Essential functions’ means the fundamental job duties of the employment position the individual with a disability holds or desires. ‘Essential functions’ does not include the marginal functions of the position." The word "desires" is what carries the definition into the hiring context: the position need not be one the individual already holds. The subdivision then supplies two non-exclusive lists. On why a function may be essential, it states that "A job function may be considered essential for any of several reasons, including, but not limited to, any one or more of the following," and gives among them that "The function may be essential because the reason the position exists is to perform that function" and that "The function may be essential because of the limited number of employees available among whom the performance of that job function can be distributed." On what shows that a function is essential, the statute lists, among other evidence, "The employer's judgment as to which functions are essential" and "Written job descriptions prepared before advertising or interviewing applicants for the job."

WHAT "REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION" AND "UNDUE HARDSHIP" MEAN (GOV. CODE § 12926(P), (U))
FEHA defines "reasonable accommodation" only by example. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (p) provides that the term "may include either of the following," and then lists, first, "Making existing facilities used by employees readily accessible to, and usable by, individuals with disabilities," and, second, "Job restructuring, part-time or modified work schedules, reassignment to a vacant position, acquisition or modification of equipment or devices, adjustment or modifications of examinations, training materials or policies, the provision of qualified readers or interpreters, and other similar accommodations for individuals with disabilities." The reference to "adjustment or modifications of examinations" and to "training materials or policies" is the part of the list that most directly touches selection procedures. Courts have supplied a general formulation as well: in Scotch v. Art Institute of California-Orange County, Inc., the Court of Appeal agreed with the definition adopted in Nadaf-Rahrov v. Neiman Marcus Group, Inc., under which reasonable accommodation means "a modification or adjustment to the workplace that enables the employee to perform the essential functions of the job held or desired." The countervailing statutory term is defined in subdivision (u): "‘Undue hardship’ means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, when considered in light of the following factors," the first of which is "The nature and cost of the accommodation needed," followed by factors addressing the financial resources of the facility and of the covered entity, the type of operations and composition of the workforce, and the geographic or fiscal relationship among facilities.

THE STATUTORY LIMIT: REFUSING TO HIRE SOMEONE WHO CANNOT PERFORM THE ESSENTIAL DUTIES EVEN WITH ACCOMMODATION (GOV. CODE § 12940(A)(1), (A)(2))
The same section that forbids refusing to hire a person because of a physical or mental disability also states a limit tied to the essential duties of the job. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (a)(1) provides: "This part does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire or discharging an employee with a physical or mental disability, or subject an employer to any legal liability resulting from the refusal to employ or the discharge of an employee with a physical or mental disability, if the employee, because of a physical or mental disability, is unable to perform the employee's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform those duties in a manner that would not endanger the employee's health or safety or the health or safety of others even with reasonable accommodations." Two distinct grounds appear in that sentence: inability to perform the essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, and inability to perform them without endangering health or safety even with reasonable accommodations. Paragraph (2) states a parallel limit for medical conditions, beginning: "This part does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire or discharging an employee who, because of the employee's medical condition, is unable to perform the employee's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform those duties in a manner that would not endanger the employee's health or safety or the health or safety of others even with reasonable accommodations." In both paragraphs the phrase "even with reasonable accommodations" is what links this limit back to the accommodation duty in subdivision (m).

WHO MUST PROVE ABILITY TO PERFORM THE POSITION SOUGHT: GREEN V. STATE OF CALIFORNIA
In Green v. State of California (2007) 42 Cal.4th 254, the California Supreme Court decided which party bears the burden of proof on the ability to perform a job's essential duties in a FEHA disability discrimination case. The Court of Appeal had held that the FEHA "does not require plaintiff to prove that he is a qualified individual. Rather, the burden is on defendant to establish that plaintiff is incapable of performing his essential duties with reasonable accommodation." The Supreme Court disagreed: "we conclude that the Legislature has placed the burden on a plaintiff to show that he or she is a qualified individual under the FEHA (i.e., that he or she can perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodation)," and "we conclude the FEHA requires employees to prove that they are qualified individuals under the statute just as the federal ADA requires." Reading section 12940 itself, the court explained: "By its terms, section 12940 makes it clear that drawing distinctions on the basis of physical or mental disability is not forbidden discrimination in itself. Rather, drawing these distinctions is prohibited only if the adverse employment action occurs because of a disability and the disability would not prevent the employee from performing the essential duties of the job, at least not with reasonable accommodation. Therefore, in order to establish that a defendant employer has discriminated on the basis of disability in violation of the FEHA, the plaintiff employee bears the burden of proving he or she was able to do the job, with or without reasonable accommodation." The court added that it saw "no statutory basis for construing the FEHA any differently from the ADA with regard to a plaintiff employee's burden of proof." Its conclusion is stated in terms that reach hiring: "we conclude that under the FEHA, a plaintiff must demonstrate that he or she was qualified for the position sought or held in the sense that he or she is able to perform the essential duties of the position with or without reasonable accommodation. Juries should be so instructed." Three justices dissented. Writing for them, Justice Werdegar concluded that, although the statutory language "does not expressly assign the burden of proof, established principles of statutory interpretation demonstrate that the reading best according with legislative intent is that inability to perform the job's essential duties is a defense on which employers have the burden of proof."

A RESCINDED OFFER AND A PERCEIVED DISABILITY: GELFO V. LOCKHEED MARTIN CORP.
Gelfo v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 34 arose from a withdrawn job offer. As the Court of Appeal summarized the facts, "Gelfo was laid off as part of a reduction in force while suffering from a workplace injury. Lockheed later offered Gelfo a different position, but rescinded its offer after determining medical restrictions imposed as a result of Gelfo's back injury rendered him unable to perform the essential functions of the new position, and no reasonable accommodation was possible." The trial court found Gelfo was not actually disabled and directed verdicts against him on his accommodation and interactive-process claims; as the appellate court put it, "The trial court agreed and directed verdicts against Gelfo on his causes of action for ‘failure to accommodate’ and ‘failure to engage in the interactive process.’ The directed verdicts were a mistake." The court held: "we conclude an employer must engage in an informal interactive process aimed at effecting a reasonable accommodation, and provide a necessary and reasonable accommodation to an applicant or an employee whom it regards as physically disabled." Explaining the statutory basis, the court wrote that "[i]n addition to a general prohibition against unlawful employment discrimination based on disability, FEHA provides an independent cause of action for an employer's failure to provide a reasonable accommodation for an applicant's or employee's known disability," and that "[u]nder the express provisions of the FEHA, the employer's failure to reasonably accommodate a disabled individual is a violation of the statute in and of itself." It also stated the two principles it saw as underlying such a claim: "Two principles underlie a cause of action for failure to provide a reasonable accommodation. First, the employee must request an accommodation," and "Second, the parties must engage in an interactive process regarding the requested accommodation and, if the process fails, responsibility for the failure rests with the party who failed to participate in good faith." On the relationship between the two claims, the court observed that "[w]hile a claim of failure to accommodate is independent of a cause of action for failure to engage in an interactive dialogue, each necessarily implicates the other." Describing the function of the process in a hiring posture, the court wrote: "In sum, when an employer needs to fill a position and an applicant or employee desires the position, the interactive process is designed to bring the two parties together to speak freely and to determine whether a reasonable, mutually satisfactory accommodation is possible to meet their respective needs." It draws on Government Code section 12940, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), (e)(2), (m) and (n), and on the definitions in Government Code section 12926, subdivisions (f), (p) and (u); on the California Supreme Court's decision in Green v. State of California (2007) 42 Cal.4th 254, which holds that a FEHA disability-discrimination plaintiff bears the burden of proving he or she is a qualified individual able to perform the essential duties of the position sought or held with or without reasonable accommodation; on Gelfo v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 34, a rescinded-job-offer case holding that the duties to accommodate and to engage in the interactive process run to an applicant whom the employer regards as disabled; and on Scotch v. Art Institute of California-Orange County, Inc. (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 986, which describes what the interactive process is, how it is triggered, and what an individual must identify to recover for a failure to engage in it. Where a specific employer and applicant are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. The sheet reports what the statutes and the decisions say. It does not address whether any particular job function is essential, whether any particular accommodation is reasonable or would produce undue hardship, or whether any particular hiring decision was lawful, and it does not restate the separate rules — covered in other information sheets in this corpus — that govern pre-offer medical examinations and inquiries, post-offer examinations, physical agility testing, or religious accommodation.

FEHA states the reasonable-accommodation duty as an unlawful employment practice, and it states it in terms that name applicants. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (m)(1) makes it unlawful "[f]or an employer or other entity covered by this part to fail to make reasonable accommodation for the known physical or mental disability of an applicant or employee." The same paragraph states the outer limit of the duty: "Nothing in this subdivision or in paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) shall be construed to require an accommodation that is demonstrated by the employer or other covered entity to produce undue hardship, as defined in subdivision (u) of Section 12926, to its operation." Paragraph (2) of the same subdivision makes it a separate unlawful practice for a covered employer, in addition to the protections of subdivision (h), to "retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting accommodation under this subdivision, regardless of whether the request was granted." The word the statute uses is "known": the duty attaches to a "known physical or mental disability." A related provision addresses how an accommodation request can arise before an offer is made. Subdivision (e)(1) generally forbids an employer or employment agency to require a medical or psychological examination of an applicant or to inquire whether an applicant has a disability, but subdivision (e)(2) provides that, notwithstanding that prohibition, "an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant's request for reasonable accommodation."

Government Code section 12926, subdivision (f) provides: "‘Essential functions’ means the fundamental job duties of the employment position the individual with a disability holds or desires. ‘Essential functions’ does not include the marginal functions of the position." On what shows that a function is essential, the statute lists, among other evidence, "The employer's judgment as to which functions are essential" and "Written job descriptions prepared before advertising or interviewing applicants for the job."

expectedJSON.body: The same section that forbids refusing to hire a person because of a physical or mental disability also states a limit tied to the essential duties of the job. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (a)(1) provides: "This part does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire or discharging an employee with a physical or mental disability, or subject an employer to any legal liability resulting from the refusal to employ or the discharge of an employee with a physical or mental disability, if the employee, because of a physical or mental disability, is unable to perform the employee's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform those duties in a manner that would not endanger the employee's health or safety or the health or safety of others even with reasonable accommodations." Two distinct grounds appear in that sentence: inability to perform the essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, and inability to perform them without endangering health or safety even with reasonable accommodations. Paragraph (2) states a parallel limit for medical conditions, beginning: "This part does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire or discharging an employee who, because of the employee's medical condition, is unable to perform the employee's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform those duties in a manner that would not endanger the employee's health or safety or the health or safety of others even with reasonable accommodations." In both paragraphs the phrase "even with reasonable accommodations" is what links this limit back to the accommodation duty in subdivision (m).

expectedJSON.body: In Green v. State of California (2007) 42 Cal.4th 254, the California Supreme Court decided which party bears the burden of proof on the ability to perform a job's essential duties in a FEHA disability discrimination case. The Court of Appeal had held that the FEHA "does not require plaintiff to prove that he is a qualified individual. Rather, the burden is on defendant to establish that plaintiff is incapable of performing his essential duties with reasonable accommodation." The Supreme Court disagreed: "we conclude that the Legislature has placed the burden on a plaintiff to show that he or she is a qualified individual under the FEHA (i.e., that he or she can perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodation)," and "we conclude the FEHA requires employees to prove that they are qualified individuals under the statute just as the federal ADA requires." Reading section 12940 itself, the court explained: "By its terms, section 12940 makes it clear that drawing distinctions on the basis of physical or mental disability is not forbidden discrimination in itself. Rather, drawing these distinctions is prohibited only if the adverse employment action occurs because of a disability and the disability would not prevent the employee from performing the essential duties of the job, at least not with reasonable accommodation. Therefore, in order to establish that a defendant employer has discriminated on the basis of disability in violation of the FEHA, the plaintiff employee bears the burden of proving he or she was able to do the job, with or without reasonable accommodation." The court added that it saw "no statutory basis for construing the FEHA any differently from the ADA with regard to a plaintiff employee's burden of proof." Its conclusion is stated in terms that reach hiring: "we conclude that under the FEHA, a plaintiff must demonstrate that he or she was qualified for the position sought or held in the sense that he or she is able to perform the essential duties of the position with or without reasonable accommodation. Juries should be so instructed." Three justices dissented. Writing for them, Justice Werdegar concluded that, although the statutory language "does not expressly assign the burden of proof, established principles of statutory interpretation demonstrate that the reading best according with legislative intent is that inability to perform the job's essential duties is a defense on which employers have the burden of proof."

expectedJSON.gap: Green was not a hiring case: the plaintiff was a long-time state employee with hepatitis C who was not permitted to return to his stationary-engineer position, and the judgment reviewed was a jury verdict in his favor that the Supreme Court reversed, remanding for proceedings consistent with its decision. The language quoted from the conclusion ("the position sought or held") is the court's own wording; this sheet does not extend it to say how the burden operates in any particular refusal-to-hire case. The decision was 4-3 (Chief Justice George and Justices Baxter and Corrigan concurring in Justice Chin's majority opinion; Justices Kennard and Moreno concurring in Justice Werdegar's dissent), and the dissent is quoted here only to show that the question was contested, not as a statement of California law. Green addresses claims under section 12940, subdivision (a); it does not decide the allocation of the burden of proof on a claim under subdivision (m) or (n), and this sheet does not resolve that question. The evidentiary and instructional rulings in Green (including the exclusion of the qualified medical examiner's testimony) are not summarized.

expectedJSON.body: Gelfo v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 34 arose from a withdrawn job offer. As the Court of Appeal summarized the facts, "Gelfo was laid off as part of a reduction in force while suffering from a workplace injury. Lockheed later offered Gelfo a different position, but rescinded its offer after determining medical restrictions imposed as a result of Gelfo's back injury rendered him unable to perform the essential functions of the new position, and no reasonable accommodation was possible." The trial court found Gelfo was not actually disabled and directed verdicts against him on his accommodation and interactive-process claims; as the appellate court put it, "The trial court agreed and directed verdicts against Gelfo on his causes of action for ‘failure to accommodate’ and ‘failure to engage in the interactive process.’ The directed verdicts were a mistake." The court held: "we conclude an employer must engage in an informal interactive process aimed at effecting a reasonable accommodation, and provide a necessary and reasonable accommodation to an applicant or an employee whom it regards as physically disabled." Explaining the statutory basis, the court wrote that "[i]n addition to a general prohibition against unlawful employment discrimination based on disability, FEHA provides an independent cause of action for an employer's failure to provide a reasonable accommodation for an applicant's or employee's known disability," and that "[u]nder the express provisions of the FEHA, the employer's failure to reasonably accommodate a disabled individual is a violation of the statute in and of itself." It also stated the two principles it saw as underlying such a claim: "Two principles underlie a cause of action for failure to provide a reasonable accommodation. First, the employee must request an accommodation," and "Second, the parties must engage in an interactive process regarding the requested accommodation and, if the process fails, responsibility for the failure rests with the party who failed to participate in good faith." On the relationship between the two claims, the court observed that "[w]hile a claim of failure to accommodate is independent of a cause of action for failure to engage in an interactive dialogue, each necessarily implicates the other." Describing the function of the process in a hiring posture, the court wrote: "In sum, when an employer needs to fill a position and an applicant or employee desires the position, the interactive process is designed to bring the two parties together to speak freely and to determine whether a reasonable, mutually satisfactory accommodation is possible to meet their respective needs." The dispositive holdings were stated twice: "In sum, we hold the trial court erred in directing a verdict for Lockheed on the cause of action for failure to provide reasonable accommodation on the ground FEHA imposes on an employer no duty to accommodate an applicant or employee who is not actually disabled," and "We conclude the trial court erred in directing a verdict for Lockheed on the cause of action for failure to engage timely and in good faith in the interactive process to determine effective reasonable accommodations."

expectedJSON.gap: Gelfo is a Court of Appeal decision, not a decision of the California Supreme Court, and it reversed directed verdicts rather than deciding that the employer had violated the statute; the court did not find that any accommodation existed for the fabricator position at issue. Its holdings rest on the "regarded as" prong of FEHA's disability definitions — the court accepted that Gelfo was not "actually" disabled on his own concessions — so the decision addresses accommodation and the interactive process for a person the employer perceives as disabled; this clause does not extend the holdings beyond that. Footnote 12 of the opinion states that ability to perform the essential job duties "is not part of a prosecution based on a perceived disability" and that eliminating the element "simply places the burden of demonstrating an applicant or employee was unable to perform, even with an accommodation, on the employer, with whom it belongs"; Green v. State of California, decided the following year and summarized in the preceding clause, places on the plaintiff the burden of proving ability to perform in a FEHA disability discrimination case, and this sheet does not resolve how the two statements fit together. The parts of Gelfo addressing the timeliness of the common law wrongful-termination claim, the jury instruction and verdict form, and the punitive-damages ruling are not summarized here.

expectedJSON.body: Scotch v. Art Institute of California-Orange County, Inc. (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 986 describes both sides of the interactive process and what a claimant must ultimately show. On who starts it: "The interactive process imposes burdens on both the employer and employee. The employee must initiate the process unless the disability and resulting limitations are obvious." Quoting an earlier decision, the court added: "Where the disability, resulting limitations, and necessary reasonable accommodations, are not open, obvious, and apparent to the employer, ... the initial burden rests primarily upon the employee ... to specifically identify the disability and resulting limitations, and to suggest the reasonable accommodations." On what happens next: "Once the interactive process is initiated, the employer's obligation to engage in the process in good faith is continuous," and, quoting a federal decision, "[t]he employer's obligation to engage in the interactive process extends beyond the first attempt at accommodation and continues when the employee asks for a different accommodation or where the employer is aware that the initial accommodation is failing and further accommodation is needed." The court then resolved a split among Court of Appeal decisions about what must be proved to recover under section 12940, subdivision (n), holding: "To prevail on a claim under section 12940, subdivision (n) for failure to engage in the interactive process, an employee must identify a reasonable accommodation that would have been available at the time the interactive process should have occurred." It recognized the information imbalance but located the point of proof in litigation: "through the litigation process, including discovery, the employee must be able to identify a reasonable accommodation that would have been available during the interactive process." The court also distinguished the two statutory claims: "Section 12940[, subdivision ](m) applies even without a showing that the employer failed to engage in the interactive process," and applies "[w]here a necessary accommodation is obvious, where the employee requests a specific and available reasonable accommodation that the employer fails to provide, or where an employer participates in a good faith interactive process and identifies a reasonable accommodation but fails to provide it," while subdivision (n), "which requires proof of failure to engage in the interactive process, is the appropriate cause of action where the employee is unable to identify a specific, available reasonable accommodation while in the workplace and the employer fails to engage in a good faith interactive process to help identify one." Applying that rule to the record, the court wrote: "Unless, after litigation with full discovery, Scotch identifies a reasonable accommodation that was objectively available during the interactive process, he has suffered no remedial injury from any violation of section 12940, subdivision (n)." The elements of the companion accommodation claim were stated as requiring that the "plaintiff has a disability under the FEHA, (2) the plaintiff is qualified to perform the essential functions of the position, and (3) the employer failed to reasonably accommodate the plaintiff's disability."

expectedJSON.body: Several other information sheets in this corpus describe rules that bear on the same facts. The sheet on post-offer, pre-employment medical examinations describes Government Code section 12940, subdivision (e) — the bar on pre-offer medical and psychological examinations and disability inquiries, the conditions on a post-offer examination, and the confidentiality of the results — which this sheet does not restate. The sheet on physical ability and agility testing describes when a selection test is not a "medical examination" and the job-related, business-necessity standard applied to disability-based disparate impact. The sheet on religious accommodation in employment describes the parallel accommodation duty under Government Code section 12940, subdivision (l) and the different "undue hardship" standard that FEHA defines for religious accommodation. The sheet on discriminatory job advertisements and applicant inquiries describes what a job advertisement or application may and may not say. The sheet on pre-employment and workplace drug testing describes the separate rules that govern testing. The ADA Reasonable Accommodation Request form in the During-employment category collects accommodation-request information from a current employee, and the sheet on genetic information nondiscrimination describes the separate treatment of genetic information. This sheet does not restate any of those materials, and it does not address leave as an accommodation, workers' compensation, or any claim arising after employment begins.
